quests.hint: Listen for when she plans to move abroad.
quests.explanation: 'Next year' and 'next spring' are different timeframes - 'next year' is broader; 'next spring' specifies a season. 'She is planning to + verb' is a common structure for describing future intentions.
quests.textToSpeak: She is planning to move abroad next year.
quests.correctAnswer: She is planning to move abroad next spring.

quests.hint: Notice whether he decided to study medicine or law.
quests.explanation: 'Medicine' and 'law' are both prestigious academic disciplines, but completely different. Choosing between them represents a very different career path. 'He has decided to study...' uses the present perfect to show a recent, completed decision.
quests.textToSpeak: He has decided to study medicine at university.
quests.correctAnswer: He has decided to study law at university.

quests.hint: Focus on whether they hope to buy or rent a house.
quests.explanation: 'Buy' means purchasing property permanently; 'rent' means paying to use it temporarily. This is a very important distinction in discussions about housing. 'They are hoping to...' expresses a wish with some uncertainty about the outcome.
quests.textToSpeak: They are hoping to buy a house by summer.
quests.correctAnswer: They are hoping to rent a house by summer.

quests.hint: Listen for the second personality adjective.
quests.explanation: 'Outgoing' means sociable and confident; 'easy-going' means relaxed and not stressed. Both are positive traits but describe very different personalities. These compound adjectives are widely used in English character descriptions.
quests.textToSpeak: My best friend is extremely funny and outgoing.
quests.correctAnswer: My best friend is extremely funny and easy-going.

quests.hint: Notice whether she can be stubborn or impatient when disagreeing.
quests.explanation: 'Stubborn' means refusing to change your mind; 'impatient' means not willing to wait. Both describe negative traits that can emerge in conflict. 'She can sometimes be...' softens the description with 'sometimes' and 'can'.
quests.textToSpeak: She can sometimes be stubborn when she disagrees.
quests.correctAnswer: She can sometimes be impatient when she disagrees.

quests.hint: Focus on whether he is reliable or talented.
quests.explanation: 'Reliable' means consistently dependable; 'talented' means having natural ability. These are very different compliments. 'He is one of the most...' followed by a superlative adjective is a common structure for praising people.
quests.textToSpeak: He is one of the most reliable people I know.
quests.correctAnswer: He is one of the most talented people I know.

quests.hint: Listen for which city she got lost in.
quests.explanation: 'Tokyo' and 'Bangkok' are both large Asian cities that can be overwhelming for first-time visitors. 'She got lost on her first day' uses the past simple to describe a completed event - a natural storytelling structure.
quests.textToSpeak: She got lost on her first day in Tokyo.
quests.correctAnswer: She got lost on her first day in Bangkok.

quests.hint: Notice whether the best part of travel is food or people.
quests.explanation: 'Meeting new people' and 'trying new food' are two of the most frequently cited joys of travel in English conversation. 'The best thing about...' is a useful superlative structure for discussing favourite aspects of an experience.
quests.textToSpeak: The best thing about travelling is meeting new people.
quests.correctAnswer: The best thing about travelling is trying new food.

quests.hint: Focus on whether he takes photos or keeps a diary when travelling.
quests.explanation: 'Takes photos' means using a camera to capture images; 'keeps a diary' means writing regular journal entries. Both are travel habits. 'He always + verb + wherever he travels' is a natural generalisation structure.
quests.textToSpeak: He always takes photos wherever he travels.
quests.correctAnswer: He always keeps a diary wherever he travels.

quests.hint: Listen for how long they have been friends.
quests.explanation: 'Since they were children' and 'since they were teenagers' describe different starting points. 'They have been friends since...' uses the present perfect with 'since' - a key structure for ongoing situations that began at a specific past time.
quests.textToSpeak: They have been friends since they were children.
quests.correctAnswer: They have been friends since they were teenagers.

quests.hint: Notice whether she values honesty or trust most.
quests.explanation: 'Honesty' means telling the truth; 'trust' means believing in someone's reliability. They are related but different values. 'She values + noun + above everything' is a strong phrase for describing priorities in relationships.
quests.textToSpeak: She values honesty above everything in a relationship.
quests.correctAnswer: She values trust above everything in a relationship.

quests.hint: Focus on whether he spends time with family every weekend or every evening.
quests.explanation: 'Every weekend' and 'every evening' are both frequency expressions, but weekends happen twice a week while evenings happen daily. 'Spends quality time with...' is a warm phrase often used about family relationships.
quests.textToSpeak: He spends quality time with his family every weekend.
quests.correctAnswer: He spends quality time with his family every evening.

quests.hint: Listen for whether she finds it hard to switch off or concentrate.
quests.explanation: 'Switch off from work' means stop thinking about work; 'concentrate during work' means focus on tasks. Both are work-life balance challenges but represent opposite problems. Phrasal verbs like 'switch off' are very common in English.
quests.textToSpeak: She finds it difficult to switch off from work.
quests.correctAnswer: She finds it difficult to concentrate during work.

quests.hint: Notice whether people are choosing flexibility or remote work over high salaries.
quests.explanation: 'Flexibility' means adaptable working conditions; 'remote work' means working from home. Both are modern work preferences. 'Many people are choosing X over Y' is a natural structure for describing social trends.
quests.textToSpeak: Many people are choosing flexibility over high salaries.
quests.correctAnswer: Many people are choosing remote work over high salaries.

quests.hint: Pay attention to what improves productivity - breaks or exercise.
quests.explanation: 'Regular breaks' and 'regular exercise' both improve productivity, but through different mechanisms. 'Taking regular X actually improves Y' - the word 'actually' signals that this might be counterintuitive or surprising.
quests.textToSpeak: Taking regular breaks actually improves your productivity.
quests.correctAnswer: Taking regular exercise actually improves your productivity.

quests.hint: Listen for whether city or country life offers more opportunities.
quests.explanation: 'Living in the city' and 'living in the country' are two different statements because the subject changes who has the advantage. This is a classic debate topic in English - urban vs rural living.
quests.textToSpeak: Living in the city offers far more opportunities.
quests.correctAnswer: Living in the country offers far more opportunities.

quests.hint: Notice whether cost or noise is the biggest drawback of city life.
quests.explanation: 'Noise' and 'cost' are both frequent complaints about city living. 'Drawback' means disadvantage - a formal synonym for 'problem' or 'downside'. 'The biggest drawback of...' is a useful academic and conversational phrase.
quests.textToSpeak: Noise and traffic are the biggest drawbacks of city life.
quests.correctAnswer: Cost and traffic are the biggest drawbacks of city life.

quests.hint: Focus on which direction young people are moving.
quests.explanation: 'Leaving cities for rural areas' and 'leaving rural areas for cities' are complete opposites - they describe migration in opposite directions. This is a very important distinction. Social trends are a key topic in English discussions.
quests.textToSpeak: Many young people are leaving cities for rural areas.
quests.correctAnswer: Many young people are leaving rural areas for cities.

quests.hint: Listen for who festivals bring together - tourists or families.
quests.explanation: 'Bring families and communities together' and 'bring tourists and communities together' describe very different functions of festivals. Traditional festivals primarily serve local social bonding, while tourism is a secondary effect.
quests.textToSpeak: Traditional festivals bring families and communities together.
quests.correctAnswer: Traditional festivals bring tourists and communities together.

quests.hint: Notice whether food or music is called an important cultural tradition.
quests.explanation: Both 'food' and 'music' are central elements of culture. 'X is an important part of every cultural tradition' - learning to swap key nouns while maintaining sentence structure is a valuable language skill.
quests.textToSpeak: Food is an important part of every cultural tradition.
quests.correctAnswer: Music is an important part of every cultural tradition.

quests.hint: Focus on whether she celebrates national or cultural holidays.
quests.explanation: 'National holidays' are officially recognised by the government (like Independence Day); 'cultural holidays' relate to ethnic or community traditions. Both are types of holidays but reflect different identities.
quests.textToSpeak: She celebrates both national and religious holidays.
quests.correctAnswer: She celebrates both cultural and religious holidays.

quests.hint: Listen for whether social media or technology changed communication.
quests.explanation: 'Social media' is a subset of 'technology'. Saying technology changed communication is broader; saying social media did it is more specific. In English, choosing the right level of specificity matters for precision.
quests.textToSpeak: Social media has changed the way we communicate.
quests.correctAnswer: Technology has changed the way we communicate.

quests.hint: Notice whether she prefers physical books or print newspapers.
quests.explanation: 'Physical books' and 'print newspapers' are different types of printed reading material. Preferences for print vs digital media is a rich discussion topic in English. 'She prefers reading X to Y' is the standard comparison structure.
quests.textToSpeak: She prefers reading physical books to digital ones.
quests.correctAnswer: She prefers reading print newspapers to digital ones.

quests.hint: Focus on whether the news or media creates unnecessary fear.
quests.explanation: 'The news' refers to specific news broadcasts or articles; 'the media' is broader, covering news, entertainment, and advertising. Both can create fear, but 'the media' makes a bigger, more general claim.
quests.textToSpeak: The news can sometimes create unnecessary fear.
quests.correctAnswer: The media can sometimes create unnecessary fear.

quests.hint: Listen for whether she compares prices or reads reviews.
quests.explanation: 'Compares prices' and 'reads reviews' are both pre-purchase habits. Comparing prices focuses on cost; reading reviews focuses on quality. Both are common in modern shopping behaviour. 'Before making a purchase' is a useful formal phrase.
quests.textToSpeak: She always compares prices before making a purchase.
quests.correctAnswer: She always reads reviews before making a purchase.

quests.hint: Notice whether people prefer to buy things in person or online.
quests.explanation: 'In person' means physically visiting a shop; 'online' means via the internet. These are two different shopping methods. The addition of 'these days' in the correct answer suggests a recent shift - a common phrase for describing modern trends.
quests.textToSpeak: Many people prefer to buy things in person.
quests.correctAnswer: Many people prefer to buy things online these days.

quests.hint: Focus on whether he spends too much money or time on unnecessary things.
quests.explanation: 'Spends too much money' and 'spends too much time' both use 'spend too much', but with different resources. Time and money are the two resources most discussed in English in the context of personal habits.
quests.textToSpeak: He spends too much money on unnecessary things.
quests.correctAnswer: He spends too much time shopping for unnecessary things.

quests.hint: Listen for whether education or health is described as important.
quests.explanation: Both 'education' and 'health' are universally valued. 'Most people agree that + noun + is very important' - 'most people agree' is a hedging phrase that presents a view as widely shared without making it absolute.
quests.textToSpeak: Most people agree that education is very important.
quests.correctAnswer: Most people agree that health is very important.

quests.hint: Notice whether the government should invest in transport or renewable energy.
quests.explanation: 'Public transport' and 'renewable energy' are both areas of government investment. Both are important policy areas. 'The government should invest more in...' is a common structure in English for making policy arguments.
quests.textToSpeak: The government should invest more in public transport.
quests.correctAnswer: The government should invest more in renewable energy.

quests.hint: Focus on whether she believes in equality or freedom.
quests.explanation: 'Equality' means everyone having the same rights and opportunities; 'freedom' means having the liberty to make your own choices. Both are important values but can sometimes be in tension - a rich topic for English debate.
quests.textToSpeak: She strongly believes in the importance of equality.
quests.correctAnswer: She strongly believes in the importance of freedom.
